before.title: Periodic Fourier differentiation identity and equivalence of the derivative and Fourier-weight Sobolev norms
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then
$D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$ and
$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.
Then $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$, and there are constants
$0<c_s\le C_s<\infty$, depending only on $s$, such that
$$c_s\,N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le C_s\,N_s(u)^2 .$$
The right-hand inequality holds for every $u\in H^s$, so the two norms are
equivalent on $H^s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of compositions
$u\circ q$ of smooth maps $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ that are $2\pi$-periodic
in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of
$u\circ q$ with $u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$ $2\pi$-periodic in each
variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $k \in \mathcal{W}(n,m)$, that is
$k : m \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{i<m}k_i = n$
([[def-multinomial-coefficient]]). Then:

1. **The closed formula, in $\mathbb{N}$.**
   $$\binom{n}{k}\cdot\prod_{i<m} k_i! \;=\; n! ,$$
   so in $\mathbb{R}$ the quotient $\iota(n!)\big/\prod_{i<m}\iota(k_i!)$ is
   $\iota\binom{n}{k}$, the canonical natural of a count.
2. **The expansion, in $\mathbb{R}$.** For $x : m \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $$\Big(\sum_{i<m} x_i\Big)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k \in \mathcal{W}(n,m)} \iota\binom{n}{k}\prod_{i<m} x_i^{\,k_i},$$
   the outer sum being the sum over the finite index set $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$
   ([[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]) and the inner product the real finite
   product of [[def-finite-sum]].

As with the binomial theorem, the identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$; the
commutative-ring version is a separate statement, to be made where rings exist.
See the Remarks of [[thm-binomial-theorem]].

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

derivations.claim: (One-variable periodic integration by parts.) For smooth $2\pi$-periodic $G,H$ and each $j$, $\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}G\,\partial_jH\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}=-\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}(\partial_jG)\,H\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}$: indeed $\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_j(GH)\,dx_j=(GH)|_0^{2\pi}=0$ by the second fundamental theorem of calculus and periodicity [L3], and the product rule gives the claim; the remaining coordinates integrate out by the product-measure convention. Consequently, for every smooth $\varphi$, every $k$ and every $\alpha$, $\int \chi_kD^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha\int\chi_k\varphi\,d\mu$: induct on $|\alpha|$, moving one variable derivative from $\varphi$ onto $\chi_k$ by the one-variable identity and using $\partial_j\chi_k=ik_j\chi_k$. In particular $D^\alpha\chi_k=(ik)^\alpha\chi_k$ in the weak sense of [L2], the case $\varphi=\chi_{-l}$ tested against $\chi_k$ having Fourier coefficients $\widehat{\chi_k}(l)=\delta_{kl}$.

(The symbol bounds.) For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ put $q_k:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}|k^\alpha|^2$, where $k^\alpha=k_1^{\alpha_1}k_2^{\alpha_2}k_3^{\alpha_3}$. Then $q_k\le(s+1)^3(1+|k|^2)^s$, because $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}\le(1+|k|^2)^s$ for $|\alpha|\le s$ and there are at most $(s+1)^3$ multi-indices in the range. Conversely $(1+|k|^2)^s\le2^s(1+|k|^{2s})$, and by the multinomial expansion [L4] with $x_j=|k_j|^2$ one has $|k|^{2s}=\sum_{|\alpha|=s}\frac{s!}{\alpha!}|k^\alpha|^2\ge\sum_{|\alpha|=s}|k^\alpha|^2$; hence $(1+|k|^2)^s\le2^s(1+q_k)\le2^{s+1}q_k$, because $q_k\ge1$ (the term $\alpha=0$ equals $1$). Thus $2^{-(s+1)}(1+|k|^2)^s\le q_k\le(s+1)^3(1+|k|^2)^s$.

(The differentiation identity (a).) If $u\in H^s$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, then $D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$: a weak derivative of $D^\alpha u$ of order $|\beta|\le s-|\alpha|$ is the weak derivative $D^{\alpha+\beta}u$, because the defining test identity for the iterated derivative follows by applying the two defining identities in succession and noting that $D^\beta\varphi$ is again a smooth test function. Testing the defining identity for $D^\alpha u$ against $\varphi=\chi_{-k}$ gives $\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int u\,D^\alpha\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-ik)^\alpha\int u\,\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$, where the middle equality uses step 1.1 for the smooth test function $D^\alpha\chi_{-k}=(-ik)^\alpha\chi_{-k}$ and the last uses $(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-i)^\alpha=i^\alpha$.

(The norm bounds for $u\in H^s$.) By Parseval [L1] applied to the $L^2$ classes $D^\alpha u$, $\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2=\sum_k|k^\alpha|^2|\widehat u(k)|^2$, so the definition of the $H^s$ norm gives $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_kq_k|\widehat u(k)|^2$. Combining with step 1.2, $\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le(s+1)^3N_s(u)^2$ and $N_s(u)^2\le2^{s+1}\|u\|_{H^s}^2$, which are the right-hand inequality and the converse inequality of (b) whenever $u\in H^s$.

(Converse direction of (b): the weighted series produce weak derivatives.) Let $u\in L^2$ with $N_s(u)<\infty$. For each $|\alpha|\le s$ the sequence $k\mapsto(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$ is square-summable because $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}\le(1+|k|^2)^s$; by the surjectivity of the coefficient isometry [L1] there is a unique class $w_\alpha\in L^2$ with $\widehat{w_\alpha}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$. For a smooth real test $\varphi$, Parseval's pairing identity [L1] gives $\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\overline{\widehat{D^\alpha\varphi}(k)}=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\overline{(ik)^\alpha\widehat\varphi(k)}=\sum_k(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\overline{\widehat\varphi(k)}=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int w_\alpha\varphi\,d\mu$, where the second equality is step 2.1 applied to the smooth $\varphi$ and the third uses $\overline{(ik)^\alpha}=(-i)^\alpha k^\alpha=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha$. Hence $D^\alpha u=w_\alpha$ weakly for every $|\alpha|\le s$, so $u\in H^s$.

(Conclusion.) By step 3.1 and step 2.2, for $u$ with $N_s(u)<\infty$ the class lies in $H^s$ and satisfies $2^{-(s+1)}N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le(s+1)^3N_s(u)^2$, so (b) holds with $c_s=2^{-(s+1)}$ and $C_s=(s+1)^3$, while (a) was proved in step 2.1.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

$k : m \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{i<m}k_i = n$
([[def-multinomial-coefficient]]). Then:

   $$\binom{n}{k}\cdot\prod_{i<m} k_i! \;=\; n! ,$$

   ([[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]) and the inner product the real finite
   product of [[def-finite-sum]].

commutative-ring version is a separate statement, to be made where rings exist.

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $k \in \mathcal{W}(n,m)$, that is
$k : m \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{i<m}k_i = n$
([[def-multinomial-coefficient]]). Then:

1. **The closed formula, in $\mathbb{N}$.**
   $$\binom{n}{k}\cdot\prod_{i<m} k_i! \;=\; n! ,$$
   so in $\mathbb{R}$ the quotient $\iota(n!)\big/\prod_{i<m}\iota(k_i!)$ is
   $\iota\binom{n}{k}$, the canonical natural of a count.
2. **The expansion, in $\mathbb{R}$.** For $x : m \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $$\Big(\sum_{i<m} x_i\Big)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k \in \mathcal{W}(n,m)} \iota\binom{n}{k}\prod_{i<m} x_i^{\,k_i},$$
   the outer sum being the sum over the finite index set $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$
   ([[def-sum-over-a-finite-index-set]]) and the inner product the real finite
   product of [[def-finite-sum]].

As with the binomial theorem, the identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$; the
commutative-ring version is a separate statement, to be made where rings exist.
See the Remarks of [[thm-binomial-theorem]].

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

before.claim: (One-variable periodic integration by parts.) For smooth $2\pi$-periodic $G,H$ and each $j$, $\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}G\,\partial_jH\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}=-\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}(\partial_jG)\,H\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}$: indeed $\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_j(GH)\,dx_j=(GH)|_0^{2\pi}=0$ by the second fundamental theorem of calculus and periodicity [L3], and the product rule gives the claim; the remaining coordinates integrate out by the product-measure convention. Consequently, for every smooth $\varphi$, every $k$ and every $\alpha$, $\int \chi_kD^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha\int\chi_k\varphi\,d\mu$: induct on $|\alpha|$, moving one variable derivative from $\varphi$ onto $\chi_k$ by the one-variable identity and using $\partial_j\chi_k=ik_j\chi_k$. In particular $D^\alpha\chi_k=(ik)^\alpha\chi_k$ in the weak sense of [L2], the case $\varphi=\chi_{-l}$ tested against $\chi_k$ having Fourier coefficients $\widehat{\chi_k}(l)=\delta_{kl}$.

(The symbol bounds.) For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ put $q_k:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}|k^\alpha|^2$, where $k^\alpha=k_1^{\alpha_1}k_2^{\alpha_2}k_3^{\alpha_3}$. Then $q_k\le(s+1)^3(1+|k|^2)^s$, because $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}\le(1+|k|^2)^s$ for $|\alpha|\le s$ and there are at most $(s+1)^3$ multi-indices in the range. Conversely $(1+|k|^2)^s\le2^s(1+|k|^{2s})$, and by the multinomial expansion [L4] with $x_j=|k_j|^2$ one has $|k|^{2s}=\sum_{|\alpha|=s}\frac{s!}{\alpha!}|k^\alpha|^2\ge\sum_{|\alpha|=s}|k^\alpha|^2$; hence $(1+|k|^2)^s\le2^s(1+q_k)\le2^{s+1}q_k$, because $q_k\ge1$ (the term $\alpha=0$ equals $1$). Thus $2^{-(s+1)}(1+|k|^2)^s\le q_k\le(s+1)^3(1+|k|^2)^s$.

(The differentiation identity (a).) If $u\in H^s$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, then $D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$: a weak derivative of $D^\alpha u$ of order $|\beta|\le s-|\alpha|$ is the weak derivative $D^{\alpha+\beta}u$, because the defining test identity for the iterated derivative follows by applying the two defining identities in succession and noting that $D^\beta\varphi$ is again a smooth test function. Testing the defining identity for $D^\alpha u$ against $\varphi=\chi_{-k}$ gives $\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int u\,D^\alpha\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-ik)^\alpha\int u\,\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$, where the middle equality uses step 1.1 for the smooth test function $D^\alpha\chi_{-k}=(-ik)^\alpha\chi_{-k}$ and the last uses $(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-i)^\alpha=i^\alpha$.

(The norm bounds for $u\in H^s$.) By Parseval [L1] applied to the $L^2$ classes $D^\alpha u$, $\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2=\sum_k|k^\alpha|^2|\widehat u(k)|^2$, so the definition of the $H^s$ norm gives $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_kq_k|\widehat u(k)|^2$. Combining with step 1.2, $\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le(s+1)^3N_s(u)^2$ and $N_s(u)^2\le2^{s+1}\|u\|_{H^s}^2$, which are the right-hand inequality and the converse inequality of (b) whenever $u\in H^s$.

(Converse direction of (b): the weighted series produce weak derivatives.) Let $u\in L^2$ with $N_s(u)<\infty$. For each $|\alpha|\le s$ the sequence $k\mapsto(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$ is square-summable because $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}\le(1+|k|^2)^s$; by the surjectivity of the coefficient isometry [L1] there is a unique class $w_\alpha\in L^2$ with $\widehat{w_\alpha}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$. For a smooth real test $\varphi$, Parseval's pairing identity [L1] gives $\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\overline{\widehat{D^\alpha\varphi}(k)}=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\overline{(ik)^\alpha\widehat\varphi(k)}=\sum_k(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\overline{\widehat\varphi(k)}=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int w_\alpha\varphi\,d\mu$, where the second equality is step 2.1 applied to the smooth $\varphi$ and the third uses $\overline{(ik)^\alpha}=(-i)^\alpha k^\alpha=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha$. Hence $D^\alpha u=w_\alpha$ weakly for every $|\alpha|\le s$, so $u\in H^s$.

(Conclusion.) By step 3.1 and step 2.2, for $u$ with $N_s(u)<\infty$ the class lies in $H^s$ and satisfies $2^{-(s+1)}N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le(s+1)^3N_s(u)^2$, so (b) holds with $c_s=2^{-(s+1)}$ and $C_s=(s+1)^3$, while (a) was proved in step 2.1.
